title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM + CUDA graphs
summary: Deep technical profiling session comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on A100/H100 for throughput/latency; focused on kernel selection, CUDA graphs, KV cache behaviors, and quantization tradeoffs. Action items include running on-prem microbenchmarks, sharing kernel-level traces, and provisioning VPC test network.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-15
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Olivia Chen (Redwood SE), Jared Liu (Redwood Infra), Maya Rodriguez (Catalyst ML Infra Lead), Carlos Gomez (Platform Eng), Priya Sharma (Head of ML), Amit Sen (SRE)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining. hopefully the audio's ok, we've got a fairly nerdy agenda today — kernel level perf, tensorrt-llm vs vllm, cudagraphs and how kv cache and batching interacts.

[00:18] Maya: yeah thanks Samir. this is exactly what we asked for — our infra lead Carlos and I will jump in on the perf bits. quick context: we're running a mix of A100 80GB on prem and testing H100 on cloud, production model is a 7B-ish instruction-tuned open model right now. lower cost priority but p95 latency target is 120ms for single-turn chat.

[00:36] Olivia: ok good. i'll call out early that a lot of the latency vs throughput tradeoffs come down to kernel selection (matmul, fused attention), cudagraph warmed paths, and how the kv cache is sharded / cached across inference workers. we saw pretty different behaviors between tensorrt-llm and vllm in our labs.

[01:05] Carlos: quick question — when you say tensorrt-llm differences, is that primarily kernel libraries or execution model? we've had odd tail latency spikes when batch sizes hit 8-16.

[01:24] Olivia: both. tensorrt-llm leverages highly optimized kernels and fused attention that reduce op count, but also uses TensorRT execution/engine semantics which can be more opaque; vLLM is more scheduler-driven and can expose different batching strategies. for small batch sizes tensorrt-llm often wins p50/p95, but vllm sometimes scales better at large batch and very long sequences due to different kv cache memory handling.

[01:52] Jared: to add: cudagraphs become visible when you have a stable trace — they lower CPU scheduling jitter and launch overhead. but if your sequence length varies a lot you can end up re-creating graphs which costs. we recommend a profile pass to generate graphs for the common length distributions.

[02:15] Priya: we've got mixed sequence lengths; average 128 tokens but 20% of requests hit 512. that recreation sounds expensive. how heavy is the recompile overhead typically?

[02:34] Olivia: it depends — on H100 we measured graph creation costing 20-120ms depending on model/graph complexity; if you re-create every long request it will kill tail. the mitigation is to pre-generate graphs for the top-k length buckets (e.g., 64, 128, 256, 512) and fallback to a slower path for uncommon lengths.

[03:02] Maya: can you share numbers? like p95 token latency for 7B at batch 1 on A100 vs H100, tensorrt-llm vs vllm?

[03:21] Olivia: sure — caveat these are lab numbers: A100 80GB, 7B (fp16) single-turn, batch=1, cached KV hit: tensorrt-llm p50 25ms p95 85ms; vLLM p50 30ms p95 120ms. On H100 (faster kernels) tensorrt-llm p50 18ms p95 60ms; vLLM p50 22ms p95 75ms. Throughput at batch=8 with 128 tokens: tensorrt-llm about 1100 tokens/sec, vllm about 900 tokens/sec on same hardware.

[03:58] Carlos: those p95 numbers for vLLM line up with our spikes. what about KV cache memory use? we've had OOMs when many sessions are warm.

[04:14] Olivia: kv cache memory depends on number of concurrent sessions * seq_len * model_hidden_size. vLLM tends to keep per-session KV in GPU memory unless configured otherwise. tensorrt-llm supports more aggressive KV sharding and offloading to host memory or NVMe in some configs, but offload cost hits latency. tradeoff.

[04:39] Amit: we run strict memory limits; is there a recommended strategy to avoid OOM while keeping latency acceptable?

[04:52] Jared: common pattern: keep active session KV in GPU until a threshold (e.g., 200-500 sessions) then evict least-recently-used session to host pinned memory. combine with prefix caching for common prompts. batching helps as well — if you can accept 10-30ms additional latency window to batch, throughput and memory efficiency improve.

[05:18] Maya: about quantization — we've looked at int8 and 4-bit quant for cost. what are the perf/quality tradeoffs per your tests?

[05:30] Olivia: int8 (TensorRT int8 or PTQ) gives a ~1.6-2.2x throughput improvement vs fp16 on many kernels, with small model quality deltas if calibrated properly. 4-bit (GPTQ-like) can give 3-4x but you start seeing more generation artifacts unless retrained/calibrated. tensorrt-llm has robust int8 kernels; vLLM uses custom quant kernels (less mature but improving). for production we often recommend starting with fp16/int8 hybrid and running eval sets.

[06:05] Priya: do you have a recommended eval set size for regression detection? we need to avoid hallucination regressions.

[06:16] Olivia: typically ~1k targeted prompts across critical templates covers most regressions; Redwood integrates eval hooks that do continuous scoring. also tie alerts to quality deltas at model or prompt-level.

[06:34] Carlos: can we talk about kernel selection — i.e., when does TensorRT pick a custom fused attention vs fallback? and how does that compare to vLLM's custom kernels?

[06:47] Jared: TensorRT uses heuristics + autotune to pick kernels based on shape and hardware; for example, with hidden size 4096 it selects different matmul tiling than hidden size 2048. those heuristics are in the engine build step — you can dump engine profiles to see chosen kernels. vLLM and other OSS runtimes often use a library of optimized kernels (like Triton or custom cuda kernels) but the scheduling and memory layout differ which affects throughput.

[07:15] Maya: does Redwood expose the kernel timeline so we can map spikes to particular kernels? that's what we need to show platform folks.

[07:26] Samir: yes — we can share kernel-level timelines and the CUDA graph traces we collect in the dedicated/private flow. Olivia / Jared will attach a spreadsheet with timestamps mapping to kernels and nvprof/cupti traces.

[07:40] Carlos: perfect. also curious about multi-instance / MPS like behavior — can you colocate multiple model instances per GPU to improve utilization? any gotchas?

[07:55] Olivia: you can partition a device across multiple instances, but context switching increases overhead and reduces benefit for low-latency requests. for throughput-optimized workloads it's fine. Redwood's runtime supports device affining policies and dynamic packing; we usually recommend a single instance with batching for low-latency chat use cases.

[08:16] Priya: what about CUDA graph warmup in cold starts — do you pre-warm graphs at boot?

[08:26] Jared: yes we recommend an offline profile step on deploy to generate graphs for typical lengths. do it as part of CI/CD and cache the graphs per model + sequence-length bucket. on new models you also want a kernel autotune step so TensorRT can pick best kernels.

[08:45] Maya: is autotune destructive to startup time? we're worried about slow rollouts.

[08:53] Olivia: autotune runs at build time — it adds time to the build/compile step but not to steady-state serving. plan for minutes to tens of minutes depending on model and hardware. for enterprise customers we provide pre-built images or compiled engines to skip that step during rollout.

[09:12] Amit: network / VPC constraints — if we go private, what's the latency cost for Redis-like KV access or host memory offload across the network? we have strict network ACLs.

[09:29] Jared: host memory offload on same host is cheap. across network you'd hit 100s of micro to ms-level extra latency depending on hops. we recommend local pinned host memory or NVMe if you need eviction, and use VPC peering with private networking for control plane. Redwood Private can be deployed in customer VPC so data plane stays local.

[09:56] Carlos: good. for our on-prem A100 cluster we have NVMe local — would that be fine for KV eviction?

[10:05] Olivia: yes NVMe-backed eviction works well; it's slower so it's better for cold sessions. the runtime treats NVMe as tertiary tier after GPU and host-pinned memory.

[10:22] Maya: can you show us an example of a kernel timeline mapping to a p95 spike?

[10:30] Olivia: sure — (shares screen) this is a trace from an A100 run. you can see when the attention kernel flares up at t=2.4s corresponding to a 512-token request that forced a graph rebuild. kernel A (fused attention) took much longer because it used a fallback kernel path due to an odd sequence shape.

[10:58] Carlos: looks like a fallback to matmul gemm kernels. is there a threshold that triggers fallback?

[11:06] Jared: often when shapes are not supported by the fused kernel or when autotune hasn't seen that shape. also certain quant modes may not have fused kernels implemented, causing fallback.

[11:20] Priya: what about reproducibility — if we see a spike in production, how easy is it to recreate in lab?

[11:28] Olivia: you can replay traces if you capture the request shapes and seeding. we often recommend a captured workload replay harness that replays arrival patterns and seq lengths to reproduce tail behaviors. Redwood can help instrument that.

[11:45] Maya: let's talk numbers for quantized kernels on A100 for 7B — any concrete comparison?

[11:53] Olivia: example lab run: fp16 batch=1 p95 85ms (A100), int8 tuned p95 48ms; throughput (batch=8, 128 tokens) fp16 ~700 tokens/sec, int8 ~1300 tokens/sec. 4-bit gave ~2200 tokens/sec but regression seen on some prompts. again, depends on kernel support.

[12:20] Carlos: that's significant. ok next: batching strategies — do you recommend fixed window batcher vs dynamic adaptive?

[12:30] Jared: adaptive batching that limits max wait (e.g., 25ms) gives best tradeoff for interactive workloads. fixed window can starve low-rate customers. vLLM's scheduler is good at dynamic packing; TensorRT setups rely on Redwood's runtime to handle dynamic batching with engine reuse.

[12:52] Maya: there was a question on prefetching KV for next-turn predictions — any patterns?

[13:00] Olivia: prefetching helps if you can predict next-turn shapes; otherwise it wastes memory. more reliable is to checkpoint the last N tokens and quickly rebuild small graphs for continuation.

[13:15] Carlos: about metrics — what should we monitor to detect kernel fallbacks?

[13:23] Olivia: track kernel name distribution, engine recompile events, cudagraph creation counts, GPU util, and per-kernel latency histograms. p95 spikes often align with increased cudagraph recreation events or fallback kernel invocations.

[13:40] Maya: are these exposable via Redwood Console?

[13:46] Samir: yes we expose per-model kernel timelines, cudagraph stats, and KV cache metrics in the Console for Dedicated/Private customers. we'll include dashboard links and sample alerts.

[13:58] Amit: security: if we run Private in our VPC, can Redwood still collect traces? we need to comply with policy.

[14:08] Samir: for Private we support an opt-in telemetry model. you can push anonymized traces to Redwood or we can accept logs via S3 endpoints with customer-managed encryption. full raw traces can remain customer-only on prem if required.

[14:26] Priya: last big piece is deployment: we want to run pilot on-prem with 4 nodes A100 and then test H100 in cloud for scale. what's a sensible pilot scope?

[14:38] Olivia: pilot scope: (1) run a 1-week replay of representative traffic to capture tails, (2) run autotune + cudagraph pregen for top length buckets, (3) run quantized vs fp16 eval set, (4) run scale test for concurrency to validate OOM and eviction thresholds. Redwood will help run steps 1-3 and provide scripts for 4.

[15:00] Carlos: timeline? we want pilot in two weeks.

[15:06] Samir: doable — we recommended start on 2025-07-21 for the replay. Olivia / Jared will coordinate.

[15:15] Maya: can you summarize prerequisites for our team?

[15:21] Olivia: sure — provide access to an admin node for collection, enable NVMe host for eviction, share representative workload traces (anonymized), and grant a small test subnet for Redwood Private peering.

[15:35] Carlos: ok we'll scope that out.

[15:40] Samir: great — now open floor for detailed q&a — maybe we'll let Jared dig into kernel timelines next.

[15:50] Jared: (screen share) here's the kernel timeline — left axis time, below the kernel names. you'll see back-to-back matmul launches and then attention. note the micro-stalls where host->device memcpy queued because a cudagraph wasn't used. those stalls are where you see p95 jumps.

[16:20] Maya: is there any tuning you do at CUDA level like stream priorities?

[16:27] Jared: stream priorities help but they also increase complexity. we use high-priority compute streams for inference and lower for management ops; that reduces interference. also use pinned host memory for faster host->device transfer.

[16:44] Priya: question about mixed-precision rounding errors with int8 — do you ever see divergence across runs?

[16:52] Olivia: small nondeterminism exists but typically stable. the real issue is calibration: a bad calibration dataset yields systematic bias. we recommend a representative calibration set and running regen checks.

[17:08] Carlos: back to vLLM — you mentioned vLLM schedules better at large batch. can you explain why?

[17:16] Olivia: vLLM's scheduler was designed to pack multiple streams into a single execution efficiently and keep per-request kv offloaded when needed, plus it delays token emission to maximize packing. it trades slightly higher median for much higher overall throughput under load.

[17:35] Maya: how about model switching/fallback? e.g., switching from a quantized model to fp16 if quality drops?

[17:44] Samir: Redwood supports policy-based routing: route requests with strict quality tag to fp16 instances, and others to quantized. automatic rollback on eval regression is also supported.

[17:58] Amit: if we tie to SSO and audit logs, does Redwood log kernel-level events with user context?

[18:08] Samir: audit logs include high-level request metadata; kernel-level traces are stored separately and can be correlated via request ids but we don't store PII. we can provide correlation guidance for Private installations.

[18:25] Carlos: let's go through the action items so folks are clear.

[18:30] Samir: Olivia / Jared will share the perf spreadsheet and traces by Friday 2025-07-18. Olivia will run int8/int4 microbench and share logs by 2025-07-22. Maya to provision VPC peering and test subnet by 2025-07-20. We'll schedule the 2-hour on-prem benchmark session the week of 2025-07-21.

[18:58] Maya: sounds good. one last quick Q — do you have example dashboards for cudagraphs and kernel fallbacks we can preview?

[19:08] Samir: yes, we'll include screenshots in the follow-up.

[19:15] Carlos: thanks all, this was helpful.

[19:20] Priya: thanks, bye.

[19:22] Samir: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts and next steps.
